meta.notes: Source of truth for the main layers, tour, region cards, controls, and shared interface copy. History copy lives in public/data/timeline.json. Anchors are [lon, lat] EPSG:4326; the site projects them. verified:false entries need a fact-check pass before launch. People counts in region cards are rough and marked with ~.
honesty_footnotes: Region shapes come from utility service areas, so borders are honest but not smooth.
Zip shapes are the Census version of zip codes (ZCTAs). They are very close, not exact.
Where the map shows a blank white gap, no utility is mapped there. Much of it is wilderness.

ui.site_dek: See who coordinates the market, who sets the rules, and who owns your local wires. Then trace the decisions that built the system.
ui.map_aria: Interactive map of the United States electricity system

methodology.title: How this map was made

sections.title: Map boundaries
sections.body: Local utility territories come from the federal HIFLD dataset. The source contains more than 2,900 utilities. Wholesale market regions are built by grouping each utility under its regional market operator. Zip boundaries use Census ZCTAs, which approximate postal zip codes. Source boundaries can be rough, and white gaps indicate areas where no utility territory is mapped.

sections.title: Corrections
sections.body: Federal territory data contains stale records and overlapping shapes. Every correction is documented in the repository. Caldwell, Texas, moved from the Eastern grid to ERCOT in March 2026. A group of western utilities joined Southwest Power Pool in April 2026. Generation-only companies and other shapes that duplicate local wires utilities are excluded.

sections.title: Utility numbers
sections.body: Utility size and operating measures come from the 2024 EIA-861 annual report. A meter is a billing account. Homes, businesses, and factories all count. Texas delivery utilities require a separate EIA table because electricity sellers hold the customer accounts there. A missing report stays blank instead of becoming zero.

sections.title: Size view
sections.body: The size view turns each utility into a circle. Circle area represents meters, electricity delivered, revenue, or customer-owned solar. Circles begin near the real utility territory and move apart until they stop overlapping. Area remains proportional to the measure. Position becomes approximate. A minimum circle size keeps small utilities visible.

sections.title: Reliability, solar, and smart meters
sections.body: Reliability reports cover utilities serving about four fifths of the country's meters. Major storms are shown separately. Customer-owned solar combines EIA net-metering and non-net-metering reports so states such as Texas are represented. It excludes utility-scale solar farms. Smart meter share compares advanced meters with all meters served by the utility.

sections.title: Electricity prices
sections.body: The combined price map works where one utility sells electricity and delivers it. ERCOT is blank because separate companies perform those jobs. The delivery map shows only the charge for poles and wires. Few utilities report that charge separately because most states still use one combined bill. State-level household prices provide the cleanest comparison of what residents pay.

sections.title: History
sections.body: The history layer contains ten dated snapshots. It does not invent annual boundaries between the surviving source dates. The 1900 map uses city power stations. The 1925 and 1932 maps trace Federal Trade Commission hatch patterns onto modern counties while preserving uncertain readings. Later maps distinguish the three synchronized grids from the regional wholesale markets operating inside them.

sections.title: Sources and uncertainty
sections.body: History cards link to original maps, laws, reports, and tables. Unverified event cards are labeled as drafts. Approximate counts use a tilde. Historical boundaries, modern utility territories, and archival hatch patterns all carry limits explained beside the relevant map.

sections.title: About
sections.body: This is part of a series about electricity markets. I work at Light, a company whose business depends on retail electricity choice. That experience informs the questions in this project. The code, data, sources, and corrections are public.

methodology.source_link: View the code, data, and corrections on GitHub ↗

wholesale.title: Markets
wholesale.explainer: Regional market operators coordinate electricity sold between power companies. They also balance supply and demand across the high-voltage grid. They do not own most power plants or local wires. About a third of the country has no regional market operator.

rules.title: State rules
rules.gloss: can you choose your electricity seller?
rules.explainer: Each state decides whether households can choose an electricity seller. The company selling electricity may be different from the utility delivering it. In most states one utility provides both services. A state regulator approves its prices.

wires.title: Local wires
wires.explainer: Almost 3,000 utilities own the local poles, wires, and meters that deliver electricity. Investors own some. Cities and public districts own others. Co-ops belong to their customers.

you.title: Your address
you.explainer: Enter your zip code. The map will show your local wires utility, your state's rules, and the wholesale market serving the area.

history.title: History
history.explainer: Electricity began as thousands of isolated city systems. Companies consolidated them. Federal law broke the largest empires apart. Engineers connected the country into three physical grids, and regional markets arrived decades later.

tour.title: Wholesale markets
tour.body: The colors show regional market operators. They coordinate wholesale trading and balance supply with demand. Gray areas have no regional market operator.

tour.title: State rules
tour.body: States decide whether households can choose an electricity seller. Dark green states allow broad choice. Pale states keep one local utility as the seller.

tour.title: Local wires
tour.body: Each shape is a utility territory. Almost 3,000 utilities own the poles and wires that deliver electricity. The colors show who owns each utility.

tour.title: Your address
tour.body: Enter your zip code. The map shows the local wires utility, the state rules, and the wholesale market serving that area.

tour.title: How the system formed
tour.body: Move through ten dated maps from 1900 to today. Each map explains one change in ownership, law, engineering, or market structure.

PJM.name: PJM
PJM.body: PJM coordinates the wholesale power market across parts of 13 states and Washington, DC. Its territory stretches from Chicago to the Atlantic coast. It is the largest regional market operator in the country.
PJM.choice: Can households choose an electricity seller? In most PJM states, yes.

ERCOT.name: ERCOT
ERCOT.body: ERCOT coordinates the wholesale market and physical grid for most of Texas. It keeps supply and demand matched every second. It owns neither the power plants nor the local wires. Most of its grid remains separate from the rest of the country.
ERCOT.choice: Can households choose an electricity seller? In most of ERCOT, yes.

MISO.name: MISO
MISO.body: MISO coordinates the wholesale power market across parts of about 15 states. Its territory reaches from Minnesota to Louisiana.
MISO.choice: Can households choose an electricity seller? Usually no. Most areas have one local utility.

SPP.name: SPP
SPP.body: Southwest Power Pool coordinates a wholesale market across the central United States. Its eastern territory reaches from the Dakotas through Kansas and Oklahoma into the Texas Panhandle.
SPP.choice: Can households choose an electricity seller? Usually no. Most areas have one local utility.

CAISO.name: CAISO
CAISO.body: CAISO coordinates the wholesale market across most of California. Several city-owned utilities remain outside it. California opened retail electricity sales in the 1990s and restricted them after the 2000 crisis.
CAISO.choice: Can households choose an electricity seller? Usually no. Many communities choose a seller on behalf of their residents.

NYISO.name: NYISO
NYISO.body: NYISO coordinates the wholesale power market across New York State.
NYISO.choice: Can households choose an electricity seller? Yes.

ISONE.name: ISO-NE
ISONE.body: ISO New England coordinates the wholesale power market across all six New England states.
ISONE.choice: Can households choose an electricity seller? Yes, in most of New England.

SPPWEST.name: SPP West
SPPWEST.body: In April 2026, western utilities opened a second market run by Southwest Power Pool. SPP now operates markets on both the Eastern and Western grids. The two physical grids remain separate and exchange limited power through converter stations.
SPPWEST.choice: Can households choose an electricity seller? Usually no.

NONE.name: No regional market

NONE_W.label: NO REGIONAL MARKET
NONE_W.body: Most western utilities remain outside a regional wholesale market. A utility may generate electricity, move it over high-voltage lines, and sell it to customers. State regulators approve its prices. Some western utilities joined SPP's new market in 2026.

NONE_SE.label: NO REGIONAL MARKET
NONE_SE.body: Most southeastern utilities remain outside a regional wholesale market. Large utilities often generate, transmit, and sell electricity. Customers receive one bill, and state regulators approve the prices.

NONE.choice: Can households choose an electricity seller? Usually no.

INVESTOR OWNED.label: Investor-owned
INVESTOR OWNED.body: Investors own this wires utility. It answers to shareholders, while state regulators approve the prices it charges.

COOPERATIVE.label: Co-op
COOPERATIVE.body: The customers own this wires utility as members of a cooperative. Co-ops serve much of rural America.

MUNICIPAL.label: City-owned
MUNICIPAL.body: A city or town owns this wires utility on behalf of the public.

POLITICAL SUBDIVISION.label: Public power district
POLITICAL SUBDIVISION.body: A local public district owns and runs this wires utility.

STATE.label: State-owned
STATE.body: A state government owns this utility.

FEDERAL.label: Federal
FEDERAL.body: The federal government runs this utility. Many federal utilities sell electricity from large dams.

NOT AVAILABLE.label: Utility
NOT AVAILABLE.body: The source data does not record who owns this local wires utility.

trivia.title: Caldwell moved from the Eastern grid to ERCOT
trivia.body: Until March 2026, Caldwell was a small pocket of the Eastern grid inside central Texas. It participated in the MISO market. New transmission lines connected the city to ERCOT's physical grid and wholesale market.

trivia.title: The Texas Panhandle uses the Eastern grid
trivia.body: ERCOT does not cover all of Texas. The Panhandle and much of the South Plains use the Eastern grid and participate in the SPP market. Lubbock moved most of its system to ERCOT between 2021 and 2023. Retail electricity choice began there in 2024.

trivia.title: El Paso is on the Western grid
trivia.body: El Paso is in Texas but outside ERCOT. Its utility operates on the Western grid. During the February 2021 freeze, El Paso avoided most of the outages that affected ERCOT.

trivia.title: Southeast Texas participates in MISO
trivia.body: The area from Beaumont north past Lufkin uses the Eastern grid and participates in the MISO wholesale market. Parts of this territory extend west of Bryan-College Station between utilities served by ERCOT.
trivia.shape_note: Entergy's own map confirms service in Burleson, Robertson, Leon, Limestone, and Madison counties; the HIFLD polygon overshoots ~20mi into Milam County (true edge is the Brazos line, ~-96.9).

trivia.title: Some East Texas co-ops participate in SPP
trivia.body: Several electric co-ops in northeast Texas use the Eastern grid and participate in the SPP market. They sit beside utilities served by ERCOT, so the physical grid boundary passes between nearby communities.

trivia.title: Some Oklahoma co-ops sit outside SPP
trivia.body: Several electric co-ops in eastern Oklahoma do not participate in the SPP market. They receive wholesale power through KAMO Power, part of Associated Electric Cooperative. Associated balances its own system instead of joining a regional market operator.

trivia.title: Nebraska spans two physical grids
trivia.body: The Eastern and Western grids meet in Nebraska. The panhandle uses the Western grid. Most of the state uses the Eastern grid. SPP now operates wholesale markets on both sides, but electricity crosses the boundary only through converter stations such as the one near Sidney.

trivia.title: Northern Maine connects through Canada
trivia.body: Northern and eastern Maine are not directly connected to the rest of New England's grid. The area connects through New Brunswick, Canada. Reaching the rest of the United States requires crossing the international border twice. ISO New England is planning a direct connection.

trivia.title: Los Angeles remains outside CAISO
trivia.body: The Los Angeles Department of Water and Power operates its own balancing area. It does not participate as a member of CAISO's regional wholesale market, which creates the large gap on this map.

trivia.title: Sacramento also operates outside CAISO
trivia.body: Sacramento's city-owned utility belongs to a separate balancing authority with several neighboring utilities. It trades electricity through CAISO programs but remains outside CAISO's main balancing area.

trivia.title: North Dakota is split between two markets
trivia.body: Utilities in eastern North Dakota participate in MISO. Utilities in the west participate in SPP. The western system, including Basin Electric and federal transmission lines, joined SPP in 2015. Both markets operate on the Eastern grid.

trivia.title: Southwest Michigan participates in PJM
trivia.body: Most Michigan utilities participate in MISO. An Indiana-based utility serving the state's southwest corner participates in PJM instead. Both markets operate on the Eastern grid.

cartogram.intro_body: Each utility becomes a circle. Circle area represents the selected measure. The circles begin near their real territories and move apart until they no longer overlap.
cartogram.legend_note: Circle area represents the amount. A minimum size keeps the smallest utilities visible.
cartogram.missing_note: {n} utilities report no number and are not drawn.

cust.label: Meters
cust.blurb: The number of billing meters each utility serves. Homes, businesses, and factories all have meters.

mwh.label: Electricity delivered
mwh.blurb: The electricity delivered across each utility's wires in one year. Large industrial customers can dominate this measure.

rev.label: Money collected
rev.blurb: The revenue each utility collects from customers in one year.

solarmw.label: Rooftop solar
solarmw.blurb: The solar capacity installed behind customer meters in each utility territory. This excludes utility-scale solar farms.

controls.parent_intro_body: Many local wires utilities belong to a larger parent company. Twenty parent companies own utilities serving about half of the country's meters. Pale areas are mostly city utilities and co-ops without a corporate parent.
controls.saidi_intro_body: Darker territories report more outage minutes per customer. The default view excludes major storms. Use the storm control to include them.
controls.saidi_note: A major storm can outweigh every ordinary outage in the year. CenterPoint reported 150 minutes without major storms and 4,316 minutes with them in the year of Hurricane Beryl.
controls.solarw_intro_body: Darker territories have more customer-owned solar capacity per household meter. The measure includes panels behind a customer's meter. It excludes large solar farms.
controls.solarw_note: This is an average across every household meter. It does not show the size of one installation. One thousand watts per home means roughly one home in six has panels.
controls.amishare_intro_body: A smart meter sends usage data to the utility and can receive time-based prices. Dark territories have replaced nearly every meter. Pale territories have replaced few or none.
controls.amishare_note: Adoption is concentrated at the extremes. Most utilities have replaced nearly every meter or almost none of them.
controls.rate_intro_body: Darker territories report a higher average price for electricity and delivery together. This measure works where one utility provides both services. ERCOT is blank because separate companies sell the electricity and deliver it.
controls.rate_note: This average combines homes, businesses, and factories. A utility serving large factories may appear cheaper than its household rate. Use the state map for household prices alone.
controls.delivrate_intro_body: This measure isolates the charge for poles and wires. Utilities report it separately where customers can choose an electricity seller. Most utilities send one combined bill, so most territories have no separate delivery price to report.
controls.delivrate_note: Only a few dozen utilities report a separate delivery price. A blank territory usually means the utility was never required to split the bill into electricity and delivery charges.
controls.price_intro_body: Darker means more expensive. Compare household prices, industrial prices, and separate delivery charges. Each measure answers a different question.
